question: Why does every finite subset of true arithmetic plus the sentences $c > 0$, $c > 1$, $c > 2$, and so on, have a model?
options: Because true arithmetic is complete, so it decides every sentence about $c$ there is
Because Peano arithmetic cannot prove that $c$ equals some particular numeral
It names finitely many numerals, so $c$ can be read as one more than the largest
Because the natural numbers already contain an element larger than every numeral
explanation: A finite subset contains only finitely many of the new axioms, so the ordinary natural numbers satisfy it with $c$ interpreted as $n + 1$ for the largest numeral $n$ mentioned. Completeness of true arithmetic plays no role, and no natural number exceeds every numeral, which is why compactness is needed for the whole set.

question: Nonstandard models of arithmetic exist only because Peano arithmetic is incomplete.
options: True
False
explanation: The construction uses compactness alone and applies to true arithmetic, which is complete by construction. Incompleteness supplies a second, different source, such as models of Peano arithmetic plus the negation of its consistency statement.

question: What is peculiar about a model of Peano arithmetic plus the negation of its consistency statement, as against a compactness model of true arithmetic?
options: It makes true a sentence false of the natural numbers, witnessed by a nonstandard element
It is inconsistent, since it satisfies the claim that Peano arithmetic proves a contradiction
It gets every arithmetical sentence right and is peculiar only in its order structure
Its proof of a contradiction is coded by a standard number, though it cannot be checked
explanation: The "proof of a contradiction" it contains is a nonstandard element, so no real proof exists and the model is a perfectly consistent structure believing something false. Getting every sentence right and differing only in structure is what the compactness model of true arithmetic does.

question: Why does each nonstandard element sit inside a block ordered like the integers?
options: Because the model proves that every number is either even or odd, which splits it into blocks
Because between any two nonstandard elements there is always a third
Because compactness adds one copy of the integers for each new constant it introduces
It has a nonstandard predecessor and a successor, so chains run down and up forever
explanation: The model proves every nonzero number has a predecessor, and a standard element has only standard elements below it, so the descending chain never reaches the standard part. Density holds between blocks, not within them: inside a block the elements are discretely ordered like the integers.

question: Why is there no least block of nonstandard elements?
options: Every nonstandard element has a nonstandard predecessor, which lies below it
Half of a nonstandard $a$ lies in a strictly lower block
The standard part has no greatest element, so nothing marks where the blocks start
The blocks are densely ordered, so none can be least
explanation: The model proves every number is twice another or one more than twice another, and halving a nonstandard element drops it by a nonstandard amount, into a lower block. Predecessors stay inside the same block, so they show only that blocks have no least element, not that there is no least block; and dense orders can have least members.

question: All countable nonstandard models share the order type of the natural numbers followed by rationals-many copies of the integers. What does this description leave out?
options: Nothing: two countable nonstandard models with the same order type are isomorphic
The standard part, which the description treats as one more copy of the integers
Addition and multiplication, so models with this order type can fail to be isomorphic
Whether the blocks are densely ordered, since that varies from one model to another
explanation: The order type says nothing about the arithmetical operations, and classifying countable models of Peano arithmetic up to isomorphism is a deep subject. The standard part is the initial segment like the natural numbers, and the density of the blocks is common to all such models.

question: Suppose a formula $\varphi$ held of exactly the standard elements of a nonstandard model. Which principle satisfied by the model does this contradict?
options: The least number principle, applied to $\neg \varphi$
Compactness, since $\varphi$ would separate the standard part from the rest of the model
Induction in the standard model, since $\varphi$ holds of zero and is closed under successor
The theorem that every number is even or odd
explanation: The least element failing $\varphi$ would be nonstandard, so its predecessor would be nonstandard and fail $\varphi$ too, contradicting leastness. Hence $\varphi$ also holds of some nonstandard element, and the standard part is not definable, which is why the model cannot notice its extra elements.

question: What does Tennenbaum's theorem rule out?
options: Any countable nonstandard model of PA at all
A computable presentation of the ordering of a countable nonstandard model
A presentation of the standard model on which addition and multiplication are computable
A countable nonstandard model of PA with computable addition
explanation: No nonstandard model with domain the natural numbers has a computable addition, let alone both operations computable. Countable nonstandard models exist by compactness and downward Löwenheim-Skolem, the standard model is plainly computable, and the order type alone can be presented computably: the obstruction is in the arithmetic.

question: Where does overspill enter the proof of Tennenbaum's theorem?
options: In showing that the model can define binary expansions of its elements in its own sense
In supplying a nonstandard element whose digits at standard places track one of the two sets
In showing that the two recursively enumerable sets cannot be recursively separated
In showing that every element of a recursive presentation must in fact be standard
explanation: Overspill yields an element whose binary expansion matches the membership pattern of one set at every standard position; if the operations were computable, its digits would be too, separating sets that cannot be recursively separated. That the sets are inseparable is an input from computability, not something overspill provides.

question: The objection says nonstandard models are fictions, since none can be exhibited. On the reply, what tells against this?
options: They prove results about standard structures, and their inexhibitability is itself a theorem
Someone will eventually exhibit one, once the right computable addition is found for it
First-order logic does pin down the natural numbers, so the models must be something else
The models can all be presented once one drops the requirement that their addition be computable
explanation: Transfer arguments of nonstandard analysis yield theorems about the ordinary reals, and an object provably lacking a recursive presentation is being described with precision. Tennenbaum's theorem guarantees that no computable addition will ever be found, and the reply agrees that first-order logic does not pin down the natural numbers.
